{{DISPLAYTITLE:Definitional equality}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Two kinds of equality|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Computation inside proofs}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Two terms are '''definitionally equal''' when they are equal by computation and unfolding of
definitions, without any proof. Definitional equality is not a proposition inside Lean. It is
a judgment of the theory, and Lean's kernel decides it, as far as it can, whenever it checks
a type. It is how computation enters proofs: a goal that holds by calculation is closed by
<code>rfl</code>, because the two sides are definitionally equal. This page lists the rules
that generate the relation, shows how natural-number literals are handled, describes how the
Lean kernel decides it, and states the theoretical limits: in Lean's full theory the relation
is undecidable, and the Lean kernel decides a slightly smaller one.

== The judgment and its use ==

The judgment <math>\Gamma \vdash e \equiv e'</math> says that <math>e</math> and
<math>e'</math> are definitionally equal in the context <math>\Gamma</math>. In the ideal
presentation it is an equivalence relation, closed under every term former, and generated
by the rules below.<ref name="carneiro2019">Mario Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of Lean'', MSc
thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 2019.
https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref> It does its work
through the conversion rule of
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Terms, types and judgments|Terms, types and judgments]]:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash e : A \qquad \Gamma \vdash A \equiv B}{\Gamma \vdash e : B}</math>

A term of one type also has every definitionally equal type. In particular, a proof of
<code>a = a</code>, which is what <code>rfl</code> is, is also a proof of <code>a = b</code>
whenever <code>a</code> and <code>b</code> are definitionally equal. Because the relation
includes reduction, types can be the result of computation.<ref name="refman-ts">''The Lean
Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, chapter 4, "The Type System".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/</ref>

== Reduction rules ==

Four reductions generate most of the relation. Each is named by a Greek letter by long
convention.<ref name="refman-ts" /><ref name="carneiro2019" />

* '''Beta''': applying an abstraction substitutes the argument, <math>(\lambda x : A.\, e)\,a \equiv e[a/x]</math>.
* '''Delta''': a defined constant equals its definition, with universe parameters instantiated, <math>c \equiv v</math> for <math>\mathrm{def}\ c := v</math>.
* '''Iota''': a recursor applied to a constructor reduces to the corresponding minor premise, as described on [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Inductive types and recursors|Inductive types and recursors]]. A projection applied to a constructor application reduces in the same way, and so does the lifting of a function through a quotient, applied to an element of the quotient ([[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Quotient types|Quotient types]]).
* '''Zeta''': a local definition equals its body with the value substituted, <math>(\mathrm{let}\ x := v;\ e) \equiv e[v/x]</math>.

Each holds by <code>rfl</code>:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def sq (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n

example : (fun x : Nat => x + 1) 2 = 2 + 1 := rfl                              -- beta
example : sq 3 = 3 * 3 := rfl                                                   -- delta
example : Nat.rec (motive := fun _ => Bool) true (fun _ b => !b) 3 = false := rfl -- iota
example : (let x := 5; x + x) = 5 + 5 := rfl                                    -- zeta
</pre>

The third line computes by recursion: the recursor flips a Boolean three times, starting
from <code>true</code>.

== Extensionality rules ==

Three further rules are not reductions of the left side to the right but identifications of
terms that cannot be told apart.<ref name="refman-ts" />

* '''Eta for functions''': <math>\lambda x : A.\, f\,x \equiv f</math>. A function is equal to the abstraction of its own application.
* '''Eta for structures''': for a value <math>s</math> of a structure type, a non-recursive type with no indices and exactly one constructor <math>\mathrm{mk}</math>, with fields <math>1, \ldots, n</math>, <math>s \equiv \mathrm{mk}\;(s.1)\;\ldots\;(s.n)</math>. This rule is new in the Lean 4 kernel.<ref name="lean4lean">Mario Carneiro, "Lean4Lean: Verifying a Typechecker for Lean, in Lean", in ''31st International Conference on Types for Proofs and Programs (TYPES 2025)'', LIPIcs vol. 384, pp. 2:1–2:23, 2026. https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.TYPES.2025.2 (read in the version arXiv:2403.14064v2)</ref>
* '''Proof irrelevance''': any two proofs of the same proposition are definitionally equal.

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash p : \mathrm{Prop} \qquad \Gamma \vdash h : p \qquad \Gamma \vdash h' : p}{\Gamma \vdash h \equiv h'}</math>

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example (f : Nat → Nat) : (fun x => f x) = f := rfl          -- eta, functions
example (p : Nat × Bool) : (p.1, p.2) = p := rfl              -- eta, structures
example (p : Prop) (h₁ h₂ : p) : h₁ = h₂ := rfl               -- proof irrelevance
</pre>

All three are accepted. None of these rules makes functions equal because they agree on all
arguments; that is the theorem <code>funext</code>, a propositional equality.<ref name="refman-fn">''The
Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, section 4.1.3,
"Extensionality".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Functions/</ref> Proof
irrelevance is the rule with the largest consequences, taken up in
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination|Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination]] and, below, as one source of undecidability.

== Natural-number literals ==

In the logic, <code>Nat</code> is the inductive type with constructors <code>zero</code> and
<code>succ</code>, so the number 1000 is <code>succ</code> applied a thousand times to
<code>zero</code>, and addition defined by recursion would take time proportional to the
size of its arguments. Lean's kernel does not compute this way. Natural-number literals are a
separate kind of term, stored as arbitrary-precision integers, and basic functions such as
addition, multiplication and comparison are evaluated on them by an arbitrary-precision
arithmetic library, usually GMP, instead of by unfolding their
definitions.<ref name="refman-nat">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0,
lean-lang.org, 2026, section 20.1, "Natural Numbers".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/</ref><ref name="bailey">Christopher
A. Bailey, with contributions from the Lean community, ''Type Checking in Lean 4'' (online
book), chapters "Weak and strong reduction", "Definitional Equality" and "Reduction".
https://ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4/</ref> When iota reduction needs to
see a constructor, a literal is presented as <code>zero</code> or as <code>succ</code>
applied to the literal one smaller, and literals compare equal to the corresponding
constructor terms, so the two forms remain interchangeable.<ref name="bailey" />

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem big_mul :
    123456789123456789 * 987654321987654321 = 121932631356500531347203169112635269 := rfl
theorem pow_mod : 2 ^ 200 % 7 = 4 := by decide

#print axioms big_mul
#print axioms pow_mod
</pre>

Both theorems are accepted, and Lean prints
<code>'big_mul' does not depend on any axioms</code> and
<code>'pow_mod' does not depend on any axioms</code>. The 36-digit product was confirmed by
computation, not by an axiom. The price is trust: the arithmetic primitives are part of the
Lean kernel, and the reference manual notes that if they did not agree with the definitions of the
functions they replace, soundness could be undermined.<ref name="refman-nat" />

== How the Lean kernel decides it ==

The Lean kernel decides definitional equality by an algorithm that applies the rules lazily,
reducing only as far as it must.<ref name="bailey" /><ref name="lean4lean" />

'''Weak head normal form.''' The basic operation reduces a term at its head only, never
under a binder that has no argument applied to it, until no beta, iota, zeta, projection or
delta step applies at the head. The result is the term's '''weak head normal form''': a
sort, a function type, an abstraction, a literal, a constructor application, or an
application whose head is a variable or a constant that cannot be unfolded or reduced
further.<ref name="bailey" />

'''Cheap tests.''' Several tests need little or no reduction: identical terms, sorts with
equal levels, the same constant at equal universe levels, and, by proof irrelevance, two
terms whose types are the same proposition. Applications, binders and function types are
compared component by component.<ref name="bailey" />

'''Lazy delta.''' When both sides are headed by definitions, Lean's kernel does not unfold
both completely, which would be much less efficient. It unfolds step by step, choosing which side to unfold by a '''reducibility hint'''
stored with every definition: <code>opaque</code>, <code>abbrev</code>, or
<code>regular</code> with a '''definitional height''', one more than the greatest height of
the <code>regular</code> definitions its value mentions. Lean can show both the hints and the rule that uses them:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
import Lean
open Lean Meta

def sq (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n
def quad (n : Nat) : Nat := sq (sq n)
abbrev Sq := sq

def showHints : ReducibilityHints → String
  | .opaque => "opaque"
  | .abbrev => "abbrev"
  | .regular h => s!"regular {h}"

#eval show MetaM Unit from do
  for n in [``Nat.mul, ``sq, ``quad, ``Sq] do
    let some (.defnInfo d) := (← getEnv).find? n | IO.println s!"{n}: not a definition"
    IO.println s!"{n}: {showHints d.hints}"

#eval show MetaM Unit from do
  IO.println ((← findDocString? (← getEnv) ``ReducibilityHints).getD "none")
</pre>

The first command prints <code>Nat.mul: regular 2</code>, <code>sq: regular 4</code>,
<code>quad: regular 5</code> and <code>Sq: abbrev</code>: <code>quad</code> is one higher
than <code>sq</code>, which it mentions. The second prints the documentation that Lean 4.34.1
carries for the hints; two passages of it read:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
* If `f` and `g` have the **same hint kind**:
  - Both `.opaque` or both `.abbrev`: unfold both.
  - Both `.regular`: unfold the one with the **greater** height first. If their heights are equal
    (in particular, if `f` and `g` are the same definition), first try to compare their arguments
    for definitional equality (short-circuiting the unfolding if they match), then unfold both.
* If `f` and `g` have **different hint kinds**: unfold the one that is *not* `.opaque`, preferring to
  unfold `.abbrev` over `.regular`.
...
The hints only affect performance — they control the order in which definitions are unfolded, but
never prevent the kernel from unfolding a definition during type checking.

The `ReducibilityHints` are not related to the `@[reducible]`/`@[irreducible]`/`@[semireducible]`
attributes. Those attributes are used by the elaborator to control which definitions tactics like
`simp`, `rfl`, and `dsimp` will unfold; they do not affect the kernel.
</pre>

Unfolding the higher definition first brings it down towards the lower one, which it is
built from.<ref name="bailey" /> Because the attributes do not reach the Lean kernel, a definition marked <code>@[irreducible]</code>, such as one defined
by well-founded recursion
([[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Structural and well-founded recursion|Structural and well-founded recursion]]), is still unfolded by the Lean kernel when a proof requires it.

'''Extensionality.''' When one side is an abstraction and the other is not, Lean's kernel
eta-expands the other side; when one side is a structure constructor application, it
compares the other side field by field through projections. Failures of the congruence step
are cached, which matters for performance.<ref name="bailey" /> Lean's kernel also has depth
and time limits on some of its operations, so many pathological checks stop with an error
instead of running for ever.<ref name="lean4lean" />

== Undecidability ==

Carneiro models what Lean's kernel checks as an '''algorithmic definitional equality''',
written <math>\Leftrightarrow</math>, and shows that it is sound: for two terms of the same
type, <math>e \Leftrightarrow e'</math> implies <math>e \equiv e'</math>.<ref name="carneiro2019" />
It is not complete, and in Lean's full theory no algorithm could be.

Carneiro proved in 2019 that definitional equality in Lean's theory is
undecidable;<ref name="carneiro2019" /> Abel and Coquand cite his proof, for the
accessibility predicate, and draw the consequence that typing is undecidable
too.<ref name="abelcoquand" /> The argument uses <code>Acc</code>, the inductive proposition behind well-founded recursion. Proof irrelevance
makes any proof <math>a</math> of <math>\mathrm{Acc}\;x</math> definitionally equal to
<math>\mathrm{intro}\;x\;(\mathrm{inv}\;a)</math>, a proof built from the constructor, where
<math>\mathrm{inv}\;a</math> extracts from <math>a</math> the accessibility of every element
below <math>x</math> in the relation. Since <code>Acc</code> has subsingleton elimination, a function into data can be
defined by recursion on such a proof, and the replacement unlocks one step of iota reduction.
Carneiro defines a function <math>f</math> that, at each step <math>n</math>, continues while a decidable
property <math>P\;n</math> holds and returns a fixed value when it fails, and takes
<math>P\;n</math> to say that a given Turing machine has not halted after <math>n</math>
steps, with the relation <math>></math> on the natural numbers. No proof that 0 is
accessible for <math>></math> can exist, but definitional equality must be decided in
every context, including one that assumes such a proof <math>a</math>. In that context the
chain

:<math>f\;0\;a \equiv f\;1\;a_1 \equiv f\;2\;a_2 \equiv \cdots</math>

in which <math>a_0 = a</math> and each <math>a_{n+1}</math> is the proof that
<math>n+1</math> is accessible which <math>\mathrm{inv}</math> extracts from
<math>a_n</math>, reaches the fixed value exactly when the machine halts. A decision procedure for
definitional equality would therefore solve the halting problem.

The algorithmic relation is therefore strictly smaller, and it is not transitive. In the
chain above it accepts
<math>f\;0\;a \Leftrightarrow f\;0\;(\mathrm{intro}\;0\;(\mathrm{inv}\;a))</math> by proof
irrelevance, and
<math>f\;0\;(\mathrm{intro}\;0\;(\mathrm{inv}\;a)) \Leftrightarrow f\;1\;a_1</math> by
reduction, when <math>P\;0</math> holds, but it does not accept the composite <math>f\;0\;a \Leftrightarrow f\;1\;a_1</math>:
<math>f\;0\;a</math> is already in normal form, so the algorithm has nothing to reduce, and the
intermediate term is a creative choice it does not make. Carneiro gives a second source of non-transitivity, quotients of
propositions, and shows that with the algorithmic relation in the conversion rule, typing
loses '''subject reduction''': a term can type-check while a term it reduces to does
not.<ref name="carneiro2019" />

Normalisation fails too. Abel and Coquand showed that a type theory with an impredicative
universe of propositions and a proof-irrelevant equality whose elimination does not inspect
the proof has terms with no normal form. Their counterexample, a version of the
self-application <math>\Omega</math>, runs in Lean 3.4.2, and using propositional
extensionality they gave a closed term, depending on Lean's standard axioms, that has no weak
head normal form at all.<ref name="abelcoquand">Andreas Abel and Thierry Coquand, "Failure
of Normalization in Impredicative Type Theory with Proof-Irrelevant Propositional Equality",
''Logical Methods in Computer Science'' 16(2), 2020.
https://doi.org/10.23638/LMCS-16(2:14)2020</ref> Carneiro reproduces it in Lean 4, with a
variant that makes a definitional-equality check on ordinary data fail to
terminate.<ref name="lean4lean" /> Lean 4.34.1 accepts the three definitions
below; asking for the normal form of <code>Om</code> does not finish:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
set_option linter.defProp false
def True' : Prop := ∀ p : Prop, p → p

def om : True' := fun A a =>
  @cast (True' → True') A
    (propext ⟨fun _ => a, fun _ => id⟩)
    (fun z => z (True' → True') id z)

def Om : True' := om (True' → True') id om

#reduce (proofs := true) Om
</pre>

Lean stops with <code>maximum recursion depth has been reached</code>. A recursion limit is
not itself a proof of non-termination; that <code>Om</code> has no normal form is Abel and
Coquand's theorem.

The reference manual states the position plainly. Lean's type theory lacks subject
reduction, its definitional equality is not necessarily transitive, and the type checker can
be made to run for ever. The sources are the ones described above: subsingleton elimination
and quotients of propositions, combined with definitional proof irrelevance, for the first two
properties;<ref name="carneiro2019" /> an impredicative universe of propositions with proof
irrelevance and propositional extensionality for the third.<ref name="abelcoquand" /> The
manual reports that failures of transitivity are exceedingly rare in practice, that, as far as
its authors know, non-termination has not occurred except in code written to provoke it, and
that logical soundness is not affected.<ref name="refman-kernel">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0,
lean-lang.org, 2026, section 2.3, "The Kernel".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/</ref> The last point
is the one that matters for checking proofs. These properties make Lean's kernel incomplete,
not unsound: their typical effect is a true equality that the Lean kernel cannot confirm in one step,
which can often be proved instead as a chain of propositional equalities, since
propositional equality is transitive.
